query: Design a lightweight alloy (<6 g/cm³) containing Magnesium and transition metals, constrained by the need to limit sintering temperature between 800 °C and 1000 °C to balance relative density and elemental volatility. The material currently suffers from unstable microstructures and poor functional properties (oxidation/corrosion) due to unclear phase transformation pathways and element segregation. Request a hypothesis on how to navigate this temperature window to form a dense, single-phase-like microstructure that maximizes barrier properties. Include prior evidence on the limitations of standard sintering in this regime, define the boundary where density fails or volatility occurs, and propose a falsification experiment comparing intermediate temperatures against the proposed optimum.

generation.hypothesis: A Mg-based refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) containing transition metals (e.g., Nb, Ta, V) and a minor amount of Al or Cr, processed via a two-step sintering protocol (initial consolidation at 850 °C followed by a short, controlled anneal at 925 °C), will suppress the formation of brittle intermetallic phases and volatile Mg loss, thereby establishing a dense, single-phase-like BCC solid solution with enhanced oxidation resistance compared to standard isothermal sintering.
generation.material_initial_state: A powder mixture of Magnesium (Mg) and refractory transition metals (Nb, Ta, V) with minor Al/Cr additions, exhibiting a multi-phase, segregated microstructure with high elemental volatility and poor sinterability in the 800–1000 °C range.
generation.intervention: Apply a non-isothermal, two-stage sintering protocol: Stage 1 at 850 °C for 2 hours to initiate solid-state diffusion without significant Mg evaporation, followed by Stage 2 at 925 °C for 30 minutes to promote phase homogenization and grain boundary cohesion, avoiding prolonged exposure above 950 °C.
generation.conditions: Atmosphere: Inert Argon (to prevent oxidation during sintering); Pressure: 50 MPa (Hot Pressing or SPS); Temperature Window: Strictly bounded between 800 °C and 1000 °C to balance density and volatility.
generation.structural_mediator: Dynamic evolution of local chemical order (LCO) and suppression of grain boundary segregation, facilitated by the high configurational entropy of the multi-principal element system which stabilizes the BCC solid solution against decomposition into brittle intermetallics.
generation.mechanism: The high mixing entropy of the Mg-transition metal system lowers the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation, while the controlled temperature ramp prevents the rapid volatilization of Mg (which occurs >950 °C) and avoids the formation of unstable oxide layers. The intermediate temperature (925 °C) allows for the formation of a protective, self-healing oxide layer (Cr2O3/Al2O3) upon subsequent exposure, acting as a diffusion barrier, while the initial lower temperature ensures densification without excessive grain growth or element loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: The resulting alloy will exhibit a relative density >95% with a homogeneous BCC single-phase-like microstructure, significantly reduced elemental segregation, and a 50% improvement in oxidation resistance compared to standard sintering at 950 °C, while maintaining ductility by avoiding the brittle-ductile transition regime associated with excessive chemical ordering.
generation.baseline: Standard isothermal sintering at 950 °C for 4 hours, which typically results in <85% relative density due to Mg volatility, significant elemental segregation, and the formation of brittle, multi-phase microstructures with poor corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: Density fails (porosity >15%) if sintering temperature drops below 800 °C due to insufficient diffusion; Volatility dominates (Mg loss >10%) and microstructure destabilizes if temperature exceeds 1000 °C or if dwell time at >950 °C exceeds 1 hour.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold for Mg volatility in the presence of refractory metals is not fully quantified in the provided evidence, and the specific phase stability of Mg-based RHEAs in the 800–1000 °C window is not explicitly detailed, requiring experimental validation of the LCO evolution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three batches of Mg-Nb-Ta-V-Al alloy powders. Batch A: Sintered isothermally at 850 °C for 4h. Batch B: Sintered isothermally at 950 °C for 4h. Batch C: Sintered via the proposed two-step protocol (850 °C/2h + 925 °C/30h). All sintered under identical inert atmosphere and pressure.
measurements: Phase composition (XRD to detect BCC vs. intermetallics)
Oxidation resistance (Isothermal oxidation at 800 °C for 50h, measuring weight gain)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if Batch C does not demonstrate a relative density >95% AND a single-phase BCC structure (or dominant BCC with <5% secondary phase) AND a weight gain <50% of Batch B after oxidation, OR if Batch C exhibits lower ductility than Batch A due to excessive ordering.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. Here, an unexpected ductile–brittle–ductile transition is discovered in a multiphase high‐entropy alloy (HEA) aged in an intermediate temperature regime. Unlike the classical thermal embrittlement driven by grain boundary effects, this transition originates from the dynamic evolution of local chemical order (LCO) and phase boundary (PB) configurations in HEAs. Aging within the embrittlement‐prone regime enhances chemical ordering, increases the density of ordered domains, and induces jagged PBs, collectively triggering plastic instability and the ductile−to−brittle transition. In contrast, aging outside this regime suppresses excessive ordering and promotes the formation of ductile interphase transition zones, facilitating a brittle−to−ductile recovery. The findings offer new insights into the thermal behavior of HEAs and challenge the established paradigm of thermal embrittlement. Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [ [1] ], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years [ [2] ]. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co [ [3] ].

First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [ [4] , [5] ]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [6] ]. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [ [7] ] and yield strength σ 0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [ [5] ].
